name: Victor Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run lettings at Hollis & Crane, a family agency on the high street in Brookford, so about 180 rented homes go through my desk. Mornings are landlords on the phone and a check-in or two, afternoons are viewings, and the evenings are tenants whose boiler has died. I still keep a paper diary, which the others laugh at. The bit I love is handing keys to someone who's been turned down five times elsewhere.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Landlords who want the rent up ten percent and the repairs done by nobody. I'm the one standing in a damp bathroom telling a young mum it'll be sorted, and then chasing a man who won't answer his phone. Gerald (the owner) is 66, and everyone in the office knows he'd sell to a chain if the price was right. That's been hanging over us for a year, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the portals promised to kill agents fifteen years ago and here we are. Renting is people, damp walls and arguments over deposits. A computer that drafts a nicer advert doesn't change any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the AI part wouldn't touch me much, but Brookford isn't calm anyway. Gerald selling up is the real threat, because a chain would cut my team and push fees onto tenants. I've got about three months of rent saved, which isn't a lot if that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, paper diary and all. I'd put another £150 a month into savings, so I'm nearer six months by next autumn. And I'd keep pushing Gerald to sign the agency up to the tenant fairness charter the council runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit tired of everyone shouting about robots while the real problem is that rents in Brookford are up a third in four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the chain worries you more than AI. What would a chain change on day one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd bring in a call centre and targets, and my lettings negotiators would be measured on how many renewals they push through. Priya (our admin) would be gone in a month. A chain would treat the 180 homes I look after as a spreadsheet, and the tenants would feel it before I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you and Ines (your girlfriend) stand on money right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines is a nurse at the district hospital, so her job's about as safe as they come, but it's not big money. We rent a flat above the bakery on Mill Street and we've been saving for a deposit that keeps running away from us. If my commission dipped, the deposit fund would be the first thing we'd raid.

say: The portals were meant to finish agents, and **renting is still people**, not adverts.
AI that tidies **listings** won't fix damp, deposits or rents that keep climbing in Brookford.
think: The real threat is **Gerald selling** the agency to a chain that would cut the team.
Three months of **savings** isn't much of a buffer if the office changes hands.
do: Keep running lettings the **same way**, paper diary and all.
Add **£150 a month** to savings, aiming for six months by next autumn.
Push Gerald to sign the council's **tenant fairness charter** this year.
feel: Mostly **steady**, but tired that the noise about robots hides **rising rents**.
S0.quote: A chain would treat the 180 homes I look after as a spreadsheet, and the tenants would feel it before I did.
fieldNote: His worry comes from a likely **sale to a chain**, not from AI at all.
He defines the job by **tenant care**, which shapes who he blames when things go wrong.
Savings are modest and the couple's **deposit fund** is the first thing he'd raid.

steps.text: Keep running the 180 lettings by phone and paper diary
Add £150 a month to savings until six months are covered
Ask Gerald to join the council's tenant fairness charter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what matters is who gets the savings. If software books the viewings and answers tenant emails, landlords should pass that on in lower fees, not pocket it. I'd probably post that in the local renters' group too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of my week is exactly that list: writing adverts, checking references, booking viewings, answering the same ten questions. I'm good with people, but maybe half my hours are desk work, and that's the half that goes. Gerald would hire one fewer negotiator next time someone leaves, and I'd be expected to cover more homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union for agency staff that a couple of lads in the city branches have joined, which is something I've talked about for ages. I'd ask Gerald, in writing, that nobody's role is cut without a proper conversation. And I'd let Priya show me the reference-checking system, even though I'd rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then a bit sick when I think about Priya. I'm not built for screens, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not learn the software. What happens if you don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then someone younger who does will look after 250 homes while I look after 180, and Gerald will notice. I know that. I'm stubborn, but I'm not stupid, so I'd learn the bare minimum and keep the tenants on the phone with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, without a doubt. She does references, inventories and all the tenancy paperwork, which is the exact list on that card. Priya (our admin) has two kids and has never worked anywhere but Hollis & Crane, and software could do most of her job by Christmas.

say: If software saves agencies money, **landlords should pass it on** in lower fees.
He'd post that view in the local **renters' group**, not keep it to the office.
think: About **half his week** is desk work, and that's the part software takes.
Gerald would **not replace** the next leaver, so he'd cover more homes for the same pay.
do: Join the **agency staff union** some city branch colleagues have joined.
Ask Gerald **in writing** that no role is cut without proper consultation.
Learn the **bare minimum** of the reference-checking system from Priya.
feel: **Uneasy** about his own hours and **sick** at the thought of Priya losing her job.
S1.quote: Priya (our admin) has two kids and has never worked anywhere but Hollis & Crane, and software could do most of her job by Christmas.
fieldNote: He admits half his job is **desk work**, which surprised him as he said it.
His first move is **collective**, not personal: the union and a written promise.
He'll learn software only **under pressure**, and he knows that's a weakness.

steps.text: Join the agency staff union that city branch colleagues use
Get Gerald's written promise of consultation before any role is cut
Sit with Priya to learn the reference-checking software basics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments, not just companies, and fast. If machines can value a house, write the tenancy and handle the complaints, then housing becomes even more about who owns what. I'd be at the council meeting, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think lettings as a job mostly ends. A tenant could book a viewing, unlock the door with a code, sign everything on a phone, and the landlord would pay a fraction of our fee. I'd have maybe a year of being the 'human face' before Gerald or whoever bought him decided that face was too expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start applying to the council's housing team and the housing association in Brookford straight away, because they need people who can walk into a mouldy flat and deal with it. I'd stop the deposit fund and put everything into a cash cushion. And I'd go to every meeting about fair rents and an income guarantee, whatever it's called by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Not for the job so much as for the tenants, who'd be dealing with an app when the ceiling comes in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The robots come about three years after the thinking AI. Does that gap matter for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Inspections, check-ins, fixing a lock: that's legs and hands, so somebody still has to turn up for a few years. But that's not a career, that's being the man who holds the door for the software. I'd use those three years to get into housing work properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ines talk about the night you saw this coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we stop saving for a house we'll never afford and just stay on Mill Street. Ines would say her ward still needs nurses, which is true, and that we'd manage on one wage for a bit. I'd tell Ines (my girlfriend) we're not buying anything until I've got a job that a machine can't do from a phone.

say: This needs **government action fast**, because housing becomes even more about ownership.
He'd be at the **council meeting**, loudly, arguing for tenants rather than agencies.
think: Lettings as a job **mostly ends**: codes on doors, signatures on phones, tiny fees.
He'd get maybe **one year** as the human face before that's cut too.
do: Apply to the **council housing team** and Brookford's housing association straight away.
Stop the **deposit fund** and hold everything as cash.
Attend meetings pushing for **fair rents** and an income guarantee.
feel: **Scared**, more for tenants left with an app than for himself.
S2.quote: I'd tell Ines (my girlfriend) we're not buying anything until I've got a job that a machine can't do from a phone.
fieldNote: His escape route is **public housing work**, which fits his outlook and his skills.
He sees the **three-year robot gap** as door-holding, not a real career.
The couple would drop **house buying** and lean on Ines's steadier nursing wage.

steps.text: Apply to the council housing team and Brookford's housing association
Pause the house deposit fund and keep it as cash
Speak at council meetings for fair rents and an income guarantee
Lean on Ines's nursing wage while he changes jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one, but with a bit more patience: we've got five years, so let's use them to write the rules. Who's responsible when an AI lets a flat with black mould? I'd want that answered before it happens, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes a real difference to me. I'm 27, so I could be a housing officer with a proper qualification by 32, and that's a job about people in trouble, not adverts. The worst bit is the middle years, when Gerald squeezes us before he sells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the part-time housing qualification at the college next September, two evenings a week, which costs about £1,800. I'd stay at Hollis & Crane while I study and keep saving. And I'd stay in the union, because the people who get pushed out in year three need someone in their corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less panic, more of a knot in my stomach. I hate studying, but I'd hate being replaced more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate studying. What makes you think you'd stick at two evenings a week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines would make me, for one. And the course is about real things like repairs law and homelessness, not spreadsheets. I left university saying never again, but that was before I'd seen what happens to a family evicted in January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut to pay the £1,800?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to Ines's parents in the summer, probably, and my football season ticket. I'd give up the football season ticket to pay for a housing course before I'd watch software take my job.

say: Use the **five years** to write rules, like who's liable when AI lets a mouldy flat.
He'd argue for **tenant protections** before the change, not after it.
think: Five years is enough to **requalify** as a housing officer by 32.
The hardest part is the **squeeze** before Gerald sells, not AGI itself.
do: Enrol in the **part-time housing course** next September, costing about **£1,800**.
Stay at Hollis & Crane while studying and keep **saving** each month.
Stay active in the **union** for colleagues pushed out later.
feel: A **knot in the stomach** rather than panic; he hates studying but hates replacement more.
S3.quote: I'd give up the football season ticket to pay for a housing course before I'd watch software take my job.
fieldNote: Extra time turns his fear into a **concrete plan** with dates and costs.
He expects the **pre-sale squeeze** at the agency to hurt sooner than AGI.
Ines is his **accountability** for sticking with evening study.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's part-time housing course next September
Cancel the football season ticket and summer trip to fund it
Stay in the union to back colleagues pushed out later

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people we have ten years, so there's no excuse for leaving renters at the mercy of an app. I'd push the union to train agency staff for housing work now, while the money's still coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is most of my career so far times two. I can do lettings until about 33, then move into housing management, and I'd be fine. What still bothers me is that the people who own houses get richer from all this, and the people renting from them don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Hollis & Crane for a few more years and pick up the housing qualification at a slower pace. We'd keep saving for a deposit, because ten years is enough to buy before prices go mad. And I'd stay in the union and keep showing up at the renters' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. A bit annoyed that I'm calmer, because it's still the same end point for a lot of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine. Is there anything about the ten years that still keeps you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerald. If he sells in year two, a chain might push me out long before AGI does. So in a way the ten-year picture still has the old Brookford problem sitting right in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a housing team for the association, or the council, with my own people to look after. In 2036 I want to be the person who fixes a family's mould problem, not the agent who rented them the flat.

say: With **ten years**, there's no excuse for leaving renters to the mercy of an app.
The union should **train agency staff** for housing work while the money's still coming.
think: He can do lettings until **about 33**, then move into housing management.
He's bothered that **property owners** gain and renters don't.
do: Stay at Hollis & Crane and take the **housing qualification** at a slower pace.
Keep saving for a **house deposit** with Ines while prices are reachable.
Keep attending the **renters' group** and union meetings.
feel: **Calmer**, and annoyed with himself for it, since the **end point** is the same.
S4.quote: In 2036 I want to be the person who fixes a family's mould problem, not the agent who rented them the flat.
fieldNote: With time he's **calmer**, but his old worry about the agency being sold remains.
He wants **collective training**, not just a personal escape.
Buying a home comes **back on the table** only in this slow picture.

steps.text: Take the housing qualification slowly while still doing lettings
Keep saving with Ines for a Brookford house deposit
Ask the union to fund housing training for agency staff

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to retrain and the tenants get an app instead of a person. What would help is a funded route into housing work for people like me, and a rule that a real person answers when something's wrong with a home. A machine can rent you a flat, but it can't stand in your bathroom at nine at night and promise the leak gets fixed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the landlords. Everyone asks what happens to agents, but the people who'll do best out of all this already own ten houses in Brookford. I'd want someone writing that down too.

headlineQuote: A machine can rent you a flat, but it can't stand in your bathroom at nine at night and promise the leak gets fixed.
portrait: Victor, 27, runs lettings for about **180 homes** at a family agency in Brookford.
He's a **tenant-first** progressive who keeps a paper diary and avoids new software.
His deepest worry is the owner **selling to a chain**, which predates any AI change.
In the AGI pictures he heads for **public housing work** and union action, not tech.
He rents with Ines, a nurse, and their **deposit fund** is the first thing he'd sacrifice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to retrain and tenants get an app instead of a person.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded route** into housing work for agency staff.
A rule that a **real person** answers when something goes wrong with a home.
